lead: Large IoT deployments cannot let every sensor talk to the cloud. Resource management groups nearby nodes into clusters, gives each cluster a head, and runs software agents that filter and decide locally. Gateways and cloud copies of data are synchronized so they agree. Clustering cuts gateway messages and saves radio energy. Agents reduce response time and upstream traffic. Synchronization keeps replicated state usable after disconnections. Only a few universities teach this topic. It appears in smart-city, agriculture and industrial monitoring.
prereq: You need: 5.2 for cloud routing, Unit 2 for WSN basics, and Unit 3 for network layer.

blocks.text: Clustering groups sensor nodes into sets, and each set elects one cluster head (CH). Ordinary nodes send readings to the CH; the CH aggregates and forwards one message to the gateway. The gateway sees C streams instead of N streams, where N is the node count. This cuts backhaul messages and lets nodes use short radio hops, which saves energy. Cluster size is a trade-off. A large cluster means fewer CHs and fewer gateway messages, but the CH spends more energy and may become a bottleneck. A small cluster spreads load but brings back gateway traffic. CH election uses residual battery, link quality, and rotation. A simple rule scores each node and the highest score becomes CH for one round. Then rotate. M_gw = C × (T/Δt). M_gw is gateway messages in T seconds; C is the number of clusters; Δt is the cluster head's reporting interval in seconds (the node-to-CH interval is separate). This counts CH reports only. An agent is software that acts for a node or a user without waiting for the cloud. A stationary agent runs on a node, gateway, or CH; a mobile agent moves code and state between devices. Agents do local filtering: the CH agent sends an alert when temperature crosses 45 °C instead of streaming every sample. Agents can aggregate, cache, and negotiate with neighbouring agents to share a radio channel or reduce duplicate alarms. This lowers latency and upstream bytes. Agents differ from SDN controllers (see 5.6): an SDN controller centralizes path control, while agents keep local autonomy. An agent must be authenticated before it changes settings.

Replication keeps copies of a record at the gateway and in the cloud. Synchronization is the process that makes copies agree. A version vector is a list of counters, one per replica. Replica A's vector dominates B if every counter in A is at least the matching counter in B and at least one is greater. If neither dominates, the updates are concurrent and a conflict exists. Resolution can be last-writer-wins with a synchronized clock, or an application rule such as higher-priority alarm wins. Eventual consistency means that if updates stop, all replicas converge; it does not mean a read is instantly fresh. Sync frequency controls the trade-off: syncing every 60 s gives fresh data and more messages; syncing on reconnect saves bandwidth but risks stale reads. Steps: 1. Exchange version vectors. 2. Detect domination or conflict. 3. Apply or merge. 4. Store the new vector.

examples.question: A field has 30 sensor nodes in 3 clusters of 10. Directly, each node sends a 64-byte reading to the gateway every 60 s. With clustering, each node sends the same reading to its cluster head every 60 s, and each head sends one 128-byte aggregate to the gateway every 60 s. Compare gateway inbound bytes per day (1 day = 86,400 s).
steps: Step 1: Reports per node per day = 86,400 ÷ 60 = 1,440.
Step 2: Direct gateway bytes/day = 30 × 1,440 × 64 = 2,764,800 bytes/day = 2.7648 MB/day (1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes).
Step 3: Clustered gateway bytes/day = 3 × 1,440 × 128 = 552,960 bytes/day = 0.55296 MB/day.
examples.answer: Gateway inbound falls from 2,764,800 bytes/day (2.7648 MB/day) to 552,960 bytes/day (0.55296 MB/day), one-fifth of the original (an 80% cut, 5 times fewer bytes); node-to-CH traffic still exists.
examples.check:
nodes=30
clusters=3
interval=60
day=86400
reading=64
agg=128
reports=day//interval
direct=nodes*reports*reading
clustered=clusters*reports*agg
print(direct)
print(clustered)
print(direct/1_000_000)
print(clustered/1_000_000)
print(direct/clustered)

traps: Cluster-head traffic is not free: node-to-head and head-to-gateway bytes add up; say whether you compare gateway inbound or total radio bytes.
Eventual consistency is not instant consistency; a read right after a write can be stale.
A larger cluster lowers gateway messages but can drain the head; there is no single best size.
An agent making local decisions is not an SDN controller.
Version vectors detect concurrent updates; one version number cannot order updates from different replicas.

quiz.a: A node that collects readings from cluster members and forwards an aggregate to the gateway.

quiz.q: Why can clustering cut gateway traffic but not total radio traffic?
quiz.a: The gateway gets one aggregate per cluster, but nodes still send to the CH and the CH sends onward.

quiz.q: A CH sends 200 bytes every 10 s. Bytes per day?
Version vectors are (2,1) and (1,2). Can one dominate?
quiz.a: No; neither is ≥ the other in every counter, so the updates are concurrent and need conflict resolution.
Save energy and reduce gateway messages.
The CH uses extra energy; rotation shares load so one node is not drained.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses clustering ideas in industrial wireless mesh standards such as WirelessHART and ISA100.11a, and in Zigbee cluster-tree topologies. LoRaWAN is a star-of-stars network: end devices send to gateways, and gateways are transparent bridges to a network server, so there is no cluster-head layer. Research explores energy-aware clustering with machine learning and mobile agents for edge filtering. Newer curricula link this topic to edge computing and digital twins. Search next for LEACH clustering, version vectors, conflict-free replicated data types, and mobile agent platforms.
